sections.h2: Where is Habersham County and what lies inside it?
sections.html:
Habersham County fills a corner of northeast Georgia in the Blue Ridge, where Clarkesville serves as county seat and Cornelia is the largest town. The charter dates to December 15, 1818, and the name recalls Colonel Joseph Habersham, who served in the Continental Army. Statistically the whole county forms the Cornelia, GA micropolitan area (Wikipedia).

The county measures 279 square miles, 277 of them land, and some of the Chattahoochee National Forest sits inside it. The top elevation is a knob around 4,400 feet just below the summit of Tray Mountain, which Habersham divides with White and Towns counties, and the Appalachian Trail runs along the ridge nearby. The Chattahoochee River rises in what used to be Habersham County, a point Sidney Lanier's poem about the river makes with its line about the hills of Habersham.

Habersham once spread across much of northeast Georgia. White and Lumpkin counties took land from it in 1857, Banks County in 1859 and Stephens County in 1905. Rabun, Stephens, Banks, Hall, White and Towns counties now touch it, along with Oconee County, South Carolina. Raoul is a census-designated place, while Batesville, Habersham Mills, Hollywood and Turnerville are unincorporated communities. A single public system, the Habersham County School District, covers the county, and Tallulah Falls School, Piedmont University and North Georgia Technical College are also located here.

sections.h2: What does Census data show for Habersham County?
sections.html:
Habersham counted 46,031 residents in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 50,416 for July 2025 represents growth of 9.5%. One resident in five (20.3%) is 65 or older, and 9.4% are foreign-born.

The long view shows steady climbing. Habersham had 3,145 residents in 1820, 18,116 in 1960, 35,902 in 2000 and 43,041 in 2010 before the 2020 count of 46,031, according to Wikipedia's table of census results. Owners live in close to three of every four homes, and 390 building permits were issued in 2025, so new construction is being added to a digest of mostly established property. According to the commissioner's page, the appraisal staff arrives at values from recent sales and market conditions as of January 1, which means a house's figure can move when neighborhood sales do (QuickFacts).

sections.h2: Who does what in Habersham County property tax?
sections.html:
An elected constitutional office, the tax commissioner bills, collects, accounts for and distributes property tax, without any role in setting values or rates. The Board of Tax Assessors sets values: it began in 1968 with three members, grew to five from January 1, 1990, and its members serve three-year terms. Rates come from the county commissioners and the school board, and the state's levy is capped at one-fourth of a mill.

  • Tax commissioner: 130 Jacobs Way, Suite 202, Clarkesville, GA 30523, phone (706) 839-0120, weekdays from eight until a quarter to five, with Saturdays closed until further notice.
  • Tax assessors: phone (706) 839-0100, the number the county gives for mobile home registration questions.
  • Board of Tax Assessors meetings: the second and fourth Monday each month, starting at nine in the morning.

The assessors' board has a long to-do list that matters to sellers: it decides which properties are exempt, approves or denies Conservation Use applications and homestead exemptions, reviews tax returns, and levies penalties against property that was never returned. It also meets with taxpayers to talk through concerns, so a seller who doubts a value can ask for that conversation before listing.

Further detail sits on the commissioner's information page and the assessors' board page.

sections.h2: Which dates drive a Habersham County tax bill?
sections.html:
Real property bills leave the office by mid-August, with the commissioner's page naming August 15 for mailing and November 15 for payment in the same year. The state default of December 20 is later than that. Mobile and modular homes use a different cycle, since their bills usually go out around February 1 and the tax and location permit are tied to April 1.

A mobile home owner who misses the April 1 payment and permit faces a 10% penalty, a summons to Magistrate Court in the county, or even a sale of the home. The decal must be displayed, and registration happens at the assessors' office.

sections.h2: How does a Habersham County assessment appeal proceed?
sections.html:
Assessment notices usually arrive in spring and give an unhappy owner 45 days, counted from the notice date. A written appeal can argue taxability, value, uniformity or a refused exemption. It is filed with the Board of Tax Assessors, and it has to name the method you have picked.

Mobile homes carry an extra step on this page: if the owner still disagrees after a changed value, the county says an appeal to the Board of Equalization can follow within 21 days of that notice. The grand jury appoints the board to hear administrative appeals from the assessors' values. For a regular parcel, ask the assessors' office for forms and the exact sequence.

sections.h2: Which Habersham County exemptions and special valuations should I know about?
sections.html:
The Tax Assessor's office takes homestead applications, and anyone newly buying is asked to bring the warranty deed. A filing by April 1 covers the first year you claim; a later one is applied to the following year. Approval then renews on its own until residence, ownership or your qualifying category changes. The county reports local exemptions that take the place of state ones whenever the local amount is greater.

  • Property in genuine agricultural use can be assessed at 30% instead of 40% of fair market value.
  • Conservation Use valuation is granted in return for a covenant with the assessors to keep the land in qualifying use for ten years at least.
  • Freeport exemption for manufacturers can reach three categories: raw goods, goods being processed, and finished goods held in a warehouse for out-of-state shipment; applications are filed between January 1 and April 1.
  • A business's equipment, machinery and fixtures are assessed at 40% of fair market value.

sections.h2: What should a Habersham County seller do when tax is still due?
sections.html:
Under state law the January 1 owner is liable for the entire year, and no refund is paid for a partial year. Who actually pays is normally set in the sale contract, so start by learning the exact balance.

Call (706) 839-0120 and ask the tax commissioner what the parcel owes for the current year and earlier ones. When closing lands between the August mailing and the November 15 date, let the closing agent know whether the new bill has gone out and been paid. A mobile home bill follows the April 1 cycle and stands apart from real property. Since a homestead exemption ends when you move or ownership changes, tell the assessors after you leave and let the buyer file in their own name.

faqs.q: What day is Habersham County property tax due?
faqs.a: Payment is expected by November 15, after bills are mailed by August 15. Mobile and modular home bills typically go out near February 1, with that tax tied to April 1.

faqs.q: Where do I find the Habersham County tax commissioner?
faqs.a: Look for the Main Office at 130 Jacobs Way, Suite 202, Clarkesville, GA 30523, phone (706) 839-0120. It is open weekdays from eight to a quarter before five, and Saturdays are closed until further notice.

faqs.q: What is the time limit to appeal a Habersham County value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days, counted from the date on the assessment notice. The Board of Tax Assessors receives a written appeal that states your chosen method.

faqs.q: By when must a Habersham County homestead application arrive?
faqs.a: April 1 of the first year you claim it. Apply at the Tax Assessor's office, with your warranty deed in hand if the purchase is recent.

faqs.q: Is farmland taxed differently in Habersham County?
faqs.a: Yes, in some cases: agricultural property that qualifies is assessed at 30% of fair market value rather than 40%. Conservation Use valuation uses current-use value and requires a covenant of ten years or more with the assessors.
